claims.text: The starting material is a nanoscale coating of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers with layer thicknesses below about 100 nm and pristine interfaces.
Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading is governed primarily by the dual role of heterophase interfaces as dislocation barriers and triggers for alternative deformation mechanisms.
Severe lattice distortion and short-range order in the HEA layers exacerbate the interfaces' resistance to dislocation glide.
Changing layer thickness changes the density of heterophase interfaces.
Moderate-temperature testing suppresses diffusion-based deformation sufficiently for dislocation-mediated plasticity to dominate.
A high density of heterophase interfaces creates stress concentrators, while compositional complexity and lattice distortion hinder long-range dislocation glide.
Hindered glide causes localized dislocation accumulation at the heterophase interfaces.
Dislocation accumulation at interfaces eventually triggers secondary deformation mechanisms near those interfaces.
Initial deformation occurs through conventional dislocation glide in each FCC and BCC layer.
Lattice distortion or order imposes an energy barrier that produces dislocation pile-ups at interfaces and changes the local stress state.
The altered local stress state activates less common slip systems, including non-basal or pyramidal slip, as well as deformation twinning.
Twin-bridging phenomena contribute to progressive deformation in the FCC/BCC multilayer.
An evolving c/a or lattice-parameter ratio may correlate with the activation of secondary slip and twinning.
Multilayers with higher interface density will exhibit more dislocation pile-up and local stress concentration at interfaces than thicker-layer, lower-interface-density multilayers.
Higher-interface-density multilayers will progressively shift from typical shear slip toward pyramidal slip and twin bridging.
Higher-interface-density multilayers will show smoother stress-strain serrations and more homogeneous plastic flow at higher strains.
The proposed mechanism applies below a critical layer-thickness threshold at which interface effects dominate.
The proposed mechanism applies only when loading does not cause thermal diffusion, loss of the multilayer architecture, or phase degradation.

Similar dislocation morphologies, slip-system activity, and stress-strain responses in high- and low-interface-density samples would falsify interface-induced secondary mechanisms as the governing explanation.

contradictions.description: The stated material contains only FCC and BCC layers, but the proposed non-basal/pyramidal slip and evolving c/a mechanism is formulated for an HCP epsilon phase. No HCP phase or FCC/BCC-to-HCP transformation is included in the initial state, intervention, or boundary conditions.
